title: From IIT Kanpur to Chief Election Commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar Faces Resignation Demands
excerpt: A former Kerala-cadre IAS officer who handled Kashmir affairs and the Ayodhya trust desk now faces an INDIA bloc petition seeking his removal over alleged voter-roll deletions. The Election Commission says its decisions were unanimous.
body:
• Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, a 1988-batch Kerala-cadre IAS officer and IIT Kanpur graduate, took charge as India's 26th CEC in February 2025.
  • INDIA bloc leaders allege irregularities and voter deletions in the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls and have sought his resignation — allegations the Election Commission has rejected, saying its decisions were unanimous.
  • A Supreme Court petition by opposition leaders seeks an independent, time-bound audit of voter deletions, disclosure of Commission records and suspension of the revision while the case is considered.
  • For voters abroad, the dispute is about whether names can be removed without notice and a chance to be heard — safeguards the petition explicitly seeks.

Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar is facing sustained calls for his resignation from opposition parties, who allege irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision, or SIR, of electoral rolls. The campaign has moved from street protests in Delhi to a petition in the Supreme Court, putting the head of India's election body — and the process that appointed him — under public scrutiny.

On Monday, INDIA bloc leaders marched towards the Supreme Court and filed a petition seeking Kumar's removal, according to Livemint. Congress leaders Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi Vadra led the march, joined by Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge, Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav, Rashtriya Janata Dal leader Tejashwi Yadav and Telangana Chief Minister Revanth Reddy, The Business Standard reported. Protesters were stopped on Bhagwan Dass Road, about 600 metres from the court.

From IIT Kanpur to the Election Commission

Kumar was born on 27 January 1964 in Uttar Pradesh. He completed a BTech in civil engineering at the Indian Institute of Technology, Kanpur, completed postgraduate studies in environmental economics at Harvard University, and also studied business finance at ICFAI, according to the Livemint profile.

https://x.com/the_hindu/status/2109611169409548663

He is a 1988-batch Indian Administrative Service officer of the Kerala cadre. In Kerala he headed several departments and served as Ernakulam district collector and Cochin municipal commissioner. At the Centre he served as joint secretary in the Ministry of Defence, additional secretary in the Ministry of Home Affairs, and secretary in the ministries of parliamentary affairs and cooperation.

As joint secretary handling the Kashmir division, he oversaw work linked to the abrogation of Article 370 in August 2019. In 2020 he led a home ministry desk on matters arising from the Ayodhya verdict, including establishing the Ram temple trust.

How he became Chief Election Commissioner

Kumar took charge as India's 26th Chief Election Commissioner in February 2025, succeeding Rajiv Kumar, who demitted office on 18 February. A Law Ministry notification said President Droupadi Murmu appointed him with effect from 19 February 2025, in exercise of powers under section 4 of the Chief Election Commissioner and other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023, ANI reported via Daily Prabhat. The appointment was made hours after a meeting of the selection committee, and a separate notification appointed Haryana-cadre officer Vivek Joshi as an election commissioner.

What the opposition alleges, and what the Commission says

Opposition leaders cite alleged irregularities in the SIR. Livemint reported that their calls intensified after a report said Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had raised written objections — described as at least 14 objections over 10 months — to decisions concerning the rolls and the Commission's functioning. Those are reported allegations, not findings by a court or audit.

The Election Commission, for its part, subsequently maintained that its decisions were unanimous and that its digital systems operated under strict security protocols, according to Livemint. That denial is central to the balance of the story: the petitioners allege deletions and database changes that need auditing; the Commission says its decisions were collective and its systems secure.

The Supreme Court petition, as summarised by Livemint, seeks an independent, time-bound audit of voter deletions and database changes, disclosure of Election Commission records, suspension of the SIR while the case is considered, and safeguards against deleting electors without notice and a reasonable opportunity to be heard. Petitioners named in reporting include Kharge, Trinamool Congress leader Saugata Roy, Yadav and Tejashwi Yadav.

The Cockroach Janta Party also demanded his resignation and planned a 10 October Jantar Mantar protest, ahead of which several leaders were detained, Livemint reported.

What happens next

The immediate test is judicial. The Supreme Court will have to decide whether to order the audit, disclosure and pause that the petition seeks, and on what timetable. For electors — including non-resident Indians on rolls in India — the practical question is procedural: notice before deletion, and a chance to be heard. No court finding on the allegations had been reported in the sources for this article.
